podcast.title: Partnership with Porter Wagoner (1967-1974)
podcast.body: Dolly Parton's career began closely linked with Porter Wagoner starting in 1967. She performed on his TV show, was part of his touring company, and recorded approximately 12 albums with him. Their collaboration was formidable, with Wagoner reportedly relying on her to sell records. "Starting in 1967 Dolly's career was linked with that of Porter Wagner. She had been a performer on the Porter Wagner TV show. She was part of his touring company and she made like 12 albums with him when she asked that he let her go in 1974."

podcast.title: Departure from Porter Wagoner (1974)
podcast.body: In February 1974, Dolly Parton left the Porter Wagoner show, a move that was her launching pad but which she had outgrown, indicating her bigger plans for her career. She was nominated for CMA Female Vocalist of the Year in 1974. "Dolly Parton left the Porter Wagner show in February, which was no doubt her launching pad, but she'd outgrown him and she had bigger plans for her career."

podcast.title: Solo TV Show (1976)
podcast.body: Dolly Parton launched her first solo TV show in 1976, which was a mix of country and pop, mirroring the broader industry trend. This show was an early indicator of her future success, including her eventual move into movies. "Dolly got her first solo TV show in 1976 but you know everybody had a variety show in the 70s so that's not a huge surprise but it is a sign of things to come for her."

podcast.title: "Iron Butterfly" Nickname and $1 Million Settlement
podcast.body: Known as the "Iron Butterfly" for her business acumen and grace, Dolly Parton settled out of court with Porter Wagoner for $1 million in their contractual dispute. She later stated it took her a while to pay it off, noting that "he got the first million dollars that I ever made." "Now Dolly who is as tough as nails as a businesswoman they call her the iron butterfly but also is the epitome of grace. She settled out of court with him and she settled with him for $1 million."

podcast.title: Appearance vs. Talent
podcast.body: While much attention was often given to Dolly Parton's appearance, especially in her younger years, she acknowledged that her looks alone could only take her so far. She emphasized that her voice and, particularly, her songwriting were the true essence of her career. "Her voice and especially her songwriting. That's the essence of her career."

podcast.title: Collaboration Attempt with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Following an impressive performance on Dolly Parton's TV show with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, the trio attempted to record an album together shortly after. However, it "didn't sound right" and faced contractual issues, delaying their successful "Trio" album until 1987. "No Dolly and Emmy Lou and Linda were as impressed as anyone with how they sounded and tried to make a record not long after that. It didn't sound right and I think there were some contractual issues."

podcast.title: Contractual Dispute and Lawsuit with Porter Wagoner
podcast.body: In 1974, Dolly Parton sought to leave her contract with Porter Wagoner after seven years, despite having initially promised him five. Wagoner initially refused to release her, leading to a lawsuit in 1979 where he sued her for $3 million, seeking 15% of her net income and record royalties from 1974 to 1979, accusing her of being "selfish" and stabbing him in the back. "Wagner sued Dolly for $3 million in 1979 saying that she broke their contract and he wanted 15% of her net income between June 1974 and June 1979 and he wanted 15% of her record royalties."

podcast.title: Intentional Move Towards Pop (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: As the 1970s progressed, Dolly Parton intentionally shifted her music towards pop, a move that displeased many in country music, including Porter Wagoner. She hired Gary Klein, a producer who had worked with Barbra Streisand, signaling her deliberate effort to change her image. She famously countered critics by saying, "I'm not leaving country music I am taking it with me." "Dolly moved more toward pop as the 70s progressed which was again upsetting to many people in country music and Porter Wagner weighed in on it said he did not approve."

podcast.title: O.B. McClinton Impression
podcast.body: O.B. McClinton included an impression of Dolly Parton in his live shows to demonstrate his versatility and to avoid being perceived as merely a "carbon copy" of Charlie Pride. "I go right into an impression of Deli Parton just so they wouldn't say that I'm a carbon copy of her either."

podcast.title: Proposed Statue Replacement for KKK Leader
podcast.body: In Tennessee, there is a desire to replace a bust of an old KKK leader with a statue of Dolly Parton, reflecting a similar sentiment seen in proposals to replace Confederate statues. "just like people in Tennessee, you want to take down a bust of an old KKK leader and replace it with one of Dolly Parton."

podcast.title: Rural Southern Origins
podcast.body: Dolly Parton, like Loretta Lynn, was born poor in the rural South, specifically in Tennessee, about 14 years after Lynn. This shared background contributed to her ability to connect with fans through relatable storytelling in her songs. "Dolly Parton like Loretta Lynn was born poor in the rural south. Dolly is from Tennessee in about 14 years younger than Loretta."

xref.body: Beyond Motown, Bobby Jean Hall has an impressive client list that includes a diverse range of legendary artists.
